claim: On Python 3.11 and 3.12, `async with asyncio.timeout(WORKER_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S): await slot.acquire()` raises the builtin `TimeoutError` (caught by `except TimeoutError`) when the deadline passes, and lets an outside cancellation propagate as `CancelledError` rather than converting it to `TimeoutError`, so a cancelled waiter is never reported as a rejection.
verify_hint: Check `asyncio.Timeout.__aexit__` converts only its own scheduled cancellation into `TimeoutError` (via `uncancel`) and re-raises an external `CancelledError`; confirm `asyncio.TimeoutError is TimeoutError` on 3.11+ and that pyproject requires Python >= 3.11 so `asyncio.timeout` exists.

In sql_threads.py:136-175, SqlWorkersBusyError is raised only at 159, in the slot wait before the executor submit at 165, so func has not started. It cannot be raised from inside func. Absolute-claim input considered: a rejected call under saturation. That call raises before anything runs, so the docstring holds.

claim: The `_fresh_sql_executor` fixture gives each test in the file a new executor by setting `sql_threads._executor` to None (so `_get_executor` builds a fresh one) and shuts down the one created at teardown; monkeypatch restores the previous executor afterward.

evidence: Fixture at tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:125-133 is autouse and module-level, so it covers every test in the file, including the runner tests above line 120. It does monkeypatch.setattr(sql_threads, '_executor', None) before the yield. sql_threads.py:85 defines the module global _executor, and _get_executor (92-99) declares it global and builds a ThreadPoolExecutor when it is None. After the yield the fixture calls shutdown(wait=False) on whatever executor the test created. The fixture takes monkeypatch as a parameter, so pytest tears monkeypatch down after the fixture's own teardown, which restores the previous value. shutdown(wait=False) does not block, and the pool tests release their holders in finally blocks. Any thread left over belongs to a discarded executor, and the next test gets a fresh one, so a later test cannot see it.

claim: `test_sql_pool_drops_a_call_cancelled_in_the_tick_its_slot_is_granted` reproduces the same-tick grant-and-cancel: after three `sleep(0)` the queued call is waiting in `Semaphore.acquire`, `slot.release()` wakes it, `queued.cancel()` lands in the same tick, and the test asserts the caller is cancelled, `ran == []` and the slot is not locked.
verify_against: `run_blocking_sql` in sql_threads.py and stdlib `asyncio.locks.Semaphore.acquire`/`release` on 3.11 and 3.12
verify_hint: Check that releasing the slot from the test (an extra release not tied to a holder) does not leave the semaphore value above SQL_WORKER_THREADS after holders finish, and that `assert not slot.locked()` after `asyncio.wait` reflects the cancelled waiter returning its slot rather than the test's own extra release.
evidence: Test (tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:296-318) fills the pool with extra=0 (value 0, locked). The queued run_blocking_sql task, on the first sleep(0), sees slot.locked() (sql_threads.py:147), enters asyncio.timeout and awaits slot.acquire() (152-153); the other two sleeps are harmless. slot.release() then does _value+=1 and _wake_up_next, which sets the waiter result and decrements _value to 0 (locked still true). queued.cancel() finds the waiter future already done, so the task gets _must_cancel and CancelledError is thrown into Semaphore.acquire, whose except branch (fut not cancelled) does _value+=1 and _wake_up_next, then re-raises. That behaviour is the same on 3.11 and 3.12. So the caller is cancelled (asserted), the call never reaches submit (ran == [] asserted after holders finish), and not slot.locked() holds because the cancelled waiter returned its grant. Had the grant been kept, value would stay 0 and locked() would be True, so the assertion tells the fixed code from the buggy path. On the hint: the test's extra release leaves the semaphore at 1 after the cancel, so after holders finish it is 9, above SQL_WORKER_THREADS. The semaphore is per-loop (WeakKeyDictionary keyed by loop), so this is confined to that test's loop. The assertion reflects the waiter's returned slot, not the extra release alone, since the grant-without-return would give locked True.

claim: `test_sql_pool_release_after_its_loop_closed_is_silent` drives `_release_slot` against a really closed loop, so `call_soon_threadsafe` raises `RuntimeError` and `is_closed()` is true, and asserts no ERROR record on any logger.
verify_hint: Check that the loop is closed before `release.set()` so the done-callback runs on a closed loop, and that the INFO record awaited is emitted by `_log_call_after_cancel` after `_release_slot` (callback order of `Future.add_done_callback`).
evidence: tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:407-425: a real new_event_loop runs run_blocking_sql(hold) until started, cancels and gathers the task, then loop.close() in finally, and only afterwards release.set() (line 415). So the worker finishes after the loop is really closed. In sql_threads.py:170 the release callback is added first, immediately after submit; _log_call_after_cancel is added at line 174 only on CancelledError, so it runs after _release_slot (concurrent.futures runs callbacks in registration order). _release_slot (115-121) calls loop.call_soon_threadsafe, which on a closed BaseEventLoop calls _check_closed and raises RuntimeError; the except branch sees loop.is_closed() true and returns silently, with no ERROR log. The test waits for the INFO pool record (emitted by _log_call_after_cancel, line 129, since the future finished without exception), which can only appear after the release callback has run, asserts it is INFO, then asserts no record at level >= ERROR in caplog.records. caplog.set_level(INFO) with no logger argument sets the root logger, so records from any logger are captured. The wrap_future chain callback is harmless on a closed loop because its destination is cancelled and the loop is closed, so it returns early.

claim: `test_sql_pool_returns_the_slot_when_submit_fails` patches `submit` on the same executor instance `run_blocking_sql` uses, and its later `_fill_pool` proves all SQL_WORKER_THREADS calls start without waiting by asserting no pool log record (no saturation warning).
verify_against: `_get_executor` and the `except BaseException: slot.release()` branch of `run_blocking_sql` in sql_threads.py
verify_hint: Check `run_blocking_sql` calls `_get_executor().submit(call)` so the instance-patched `submit` is hit; check that `_fill_pool` with `extra=0` would fail (timeout assertion) or log a saturation warning if a slot had leaked, with `_last_saturation_warning` reset to None.
evidence: sql_threads.py:165 run_blocking_sql calls _get_executor().submit(call); _get_executor (92-99) returns the module singleton, and the test (test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:452,458) patches submit on that same instance via sql_threads._get_executor(), so refuse is hit and the except BaseException branch (166-168) calls slot.release(). The test resets _last_saturation_warning to None (450) and sets caplog on the pool logger (POOL_LOGGER == sqllens.agent.integrations.sql_threads, line 122). _fill_pool(extra=0) (140-169) launches SQL_WORKER_THREADS=8 holders and waits up to 5s for all 8 to run at once. Had a slot leaked, the 8th call would find slot.locked() true (147), log the saturation warning (110, not rate-limited since reset to None), and block, so fill would hit its timeout assertion and _pool_records(caplog)==[] (468) would fail. Claim holds.

claim: `test_sql_pool_logs_every_rejected_call` asserts exactly three rejection WARNINGs and four pool records in total (three rejections plus one saturation warning), with no record containing the SQL argument or the exception message's word 'busy'.
